title: Cardinals in the wilderness, plus Iran’s World Cup limbo
content:
The Pulse Newsletter 📣 | This is The Athletic’s daily sports newsletter. Sign up here to receive The Pulse directly in your inbox.

Good morning! Identify your nemesis today. Inside:

What is a baseball season like when the Cardinals aren’t relevant?

If you started following the sport around 2000 or later, you can’t answer that question. Sure, St. Louis has missed the playoffs 10 times since then, including each of the past three years. The team had narrow losing records in 2007 and last year, along with being legitimately bad (71-91) in 2023. But even then, the Cardinals were supposed to be pretty good. They carried a 67 percent shot at the postseason into the ‘23 season, per FanGraphs, and a 48 percent chance in ‘24. Last year, the Cards had been declining but still entered with about a one-in-four playoff shot in a tightly packed NL Central. The team went 78-84 and, finally, had seen enough.

This year will be a new world for the franchise. Ex-Rays and Red Sox executive Chaim Bloom took over for longtime president of baseball operations John Mozeliak after last season and got to work on a full-on rebuild, not seen here in decades. Bloom traded two of the team’s top three position players by WAR (first baseman Willson Contreras to the Red Sox, utility star Brendan Donovan to the Mariners). He sent the club’s best pitcher, Sonny Gray, to Boston in a separate deal. Third baseman Nolan Arenado, in his reduced state, is finally gone too.

The early FanGraphs projection: 75 wins, last in the Central, with an 8 percent postseason shot. The only teams with longer odds are the Marlins, Angels, White Sox, Nationals and Rockies.

The major-league team has very little in the way of good, young pitching. Bloom tried to address that for the future with his offseason roster flip. The lineup is more fun; the speedy Masyn Winn will play shortstop, likely next to Keith Law’s No. 7 prospect, JJ Wetherholt. (The second baseman should be good quickly.) Several other hitters are at least a little interesting. Meanwhile, Keith ranks the farm system 11th. Rebuilds have started in worse places.

Which begs some questions: With the lineup still decent even now, was Bloom right to start tearing things down to the studs? And will a fan base that is only used to having a competitive team accept his judgment? I asked Katie Woo, a staff writer for The Athletic who just spent five years covering the team:

💬 The Cardinals would have been justified tearing it all down a year ago, when the fall of their long-heralded player development system led to sweeping changes throughout the organization. The biggest question most Cardinals fans have now is: Why did it take so long?

The Cardinals’ rebuild has been advertised over the last year. Ownership admitted to needing to invest more in player development and acquisition, two areas where the organization had fallen drastically behind. Stadium attendance reached a record low, leading to a significant drop in gate revenue. Combine that with a scrapped television deal — St. Louis was one of several MLB teams to cut ties with FanDuel Sports Network this winter — and the timing makes sense.

Fans seem to understand the timing as well, but don’t confuse that with complacency. It helps that the Cardinals farm system has been restocked with several promising young players, and that Bloom has been honest and communicative about his operations so far. The Cardinals have not had to rebuild in over 30 years. Fans are appreciative about having a plan in place, but their grace will only extend so far — especially if the plan does not yield results.

Thanks to Katie. We’ll set the over/under for the next competitive Cardinals team at 2028.

Is Iran’s World Cup in limbo?

Obviously sports aren’t the most important thing going on right now. Yesterday’s attack on Iran and its reprisals do raise questions in this realm, though, including what it means for the Iranian team at this summer’s World Cup. The U.S. is scheduled to host all three of Iran’s group games, and while Iranian nationals are prohibited from traveling to the U.S. under President Donald Trump’s travel ban, there are exceptions for athletes. Will that change? Here’s what we know.

A touching combine moment

It’s easy to be cynical about the way the NFL combine reduces players to a series of measurements. But then you see Mike Washington Jr., from an Arkansas team that went 2-10, crying happy tears after leading all running backs with a 4.33-second 40-yard dash. It caps an offseason where Washington made a strong case to be a top-three back in the draft, per Dane Brugler, and his reaction is a joy to watch:

The Americans have won seven of the 10 editions of the SheBelieves Cup, but saw a five-year streak end last year, when Japan took the title. Here’s the rundown of the U.S. roster, from Tamerra Griffin. Coach Emma Hayes seems to be settling on a core of players she likes, as everyone on the American team has previously appeared for the USWNT.

Companies are lining up to be the Strava of tennis, capitalizing on an influx of amateur players who love data as much as pros. Charlie Eccleshare’s deep dive into the race to monetize is worth your time.

Pat Riley, the legendary NBA coach and executive, believes in the power of style — specifically, that wearing a suit makes for a more effective leader. He might be right.

If you are a fan of crispy cookies (I prefer mine roughly 5 minutes underbaked), my husband bought no less than seven bags of Dad’s Original Scotch Oatmeal crispy cookies when we stopped in St. Louis en route to Indianapolis for the NFL combine. SEVEN! — Jill Thaw

Yes, the Hawks plan to bring a “Magic City” strip club vibe to an upcoming home game — but it’s not really worth your outrage, as David Aldridge writes.

Former world-class distance runner Jeff Galloway died Wednesday at 80, but his legacy lives on in the thousands he inspired to train via the run-walk method he popularized.

Finally got into “Bone Valley” and, as many know, just an incredible pod. True crime junkies, you’re home. — Chris Sprow

As Olympic gold medalist Alysa Liu’s star continues to rise, murals in her honor are popping up in California. The latest in Oakland, which she calls home, is an ode to doing things your own way.
